Alone at Silvermount, Emmett dies with the word "Bluebell" on his lips and drops the glass snow globe on the floor. 

A newsreel obituary recaps Emmett's public life and closes without explaining his last word. 

The reporter Nash is sent to find out what "Bluebell" means and is turned away by a drunk Nora in a seaside nightclub. 

In a mining boarding house out west, long before the newsreels, Emmett Rusk's mother signed her son over to the banker Barrow after a defaulted lodger's mine deed made the family rich. The young boy drove his sled into Barrow's stomach and was taken east away from his parents anyway. On his twenty-fifth birthday, Emmett took control of the fortune and told Barrow that of all his holdings he wanted to run a failing city newspaper, the Clarion. Emmett moved into the Clarion, installed his manager Marsh and his friend Devlin, and printed a signed statement of principles on the front page. He hired away the entire staff of the rival paper and threw a party with a brass band and a chorus line. 

Emmett returned from a buying trip abroad engaged to Adele, the governor's niece. A run of breakfast-table scenes charted the marriage cooling into silence behind separate newspapers. Walking alone, Emmett met the shopgirl Nora Kell on the street with mud on his coat and started visiting her rooms in secret. Mid-campaign for governor, the party boss Halloran brought Adele to Nora's rooms and threatened exposure, but Emmett refused to withdraw. Emmett lost the election, Devlin asked to be transferred to another city, and the marriage collapsed. 

Nora's opera debut was a humiliation, and a drunk Devlin began the savage review that Emmett finished, printed, and fired him for. Afterwards, Emmett married Nora and forced her into an opera career for which she had no voice. Nora swallowed poison rather than sing again, and Emmett finally let her stop. 

Emmett shut Nora away in the half-finished palace he called Silvermount, where she worked jigsaw puzzles in the vast empty hall. After a joyless beach picnic and a quarrel, Nora packed her bags and left him. Enraged, Emmett wrecked Nora's bedroom, found a glass snow globe, murmured "Bluebell", and carried it past the endless mirrors. 

Decades later, Nash reads Barrow's memoir and interviews Marsh, Devlin, Nora, and the butler Colm before concluding that no single word explains a life, as workmen shovel a sled marked Bluebell into the furnace.

Over breakfast, the crew argued about what a pop song was really about and whether waitresses deserved a tip. 

Hours later, the job was a catastrophe. Mr. Ash drove the screaming Mr. Elm to the warehouse rendezvous, cradling him on the floorboard and swearing he was not going to die. Mr. Birch arrived soon after, arguing furiously that the job had been a setup with an informer inside it, before slipping outside to hide the diamonds.

Earlier that morning, before the violence, Bram had handed out the tree aliases, ignoring it when Mr. Birch objected to being Mr. Birch. 

Now, back in the present chaos of the hideout, Mr. Cedar strolled in and produced a kidnapped patrolman, Doyle, dragging him from the boot of his car. 

Years before any of this, Ren Vasco had walked out of prison, immediately reporting to Bram and Cal, who owed him dearly for the years he had kept his mouth shut.

Inside the warehouse, Cedar was left alone with the bound officer. He turned on a radio oldie, danced to the music, cut off Doyle's ear, and doused the weeping policeman in petrol. From his place on the floor, bleeding heavily, Elm raised his gun and shot Cedar dead. Elm whispered to the terrified Doyle that he was actually a cop and that the police were already waiting outside for Bram.

Months ago, undercover officer Danny Roarke had sat in a dim room rehearsing a fabricated anecdote about a drug bust in a public toilet with his handler Pruitt, repeating it until he could tell it as naturally as a real memory. Danny had then performed the anecdote for the boss Bram, his son Cal, and Mr. Ash. Convinced, Bram had taken him onto the crew as Mr. Elm. 

Earlier that afternoon, the robbery had collapsed within a minute. Ash had shot his way clear of the police from the getaway car with Elm beside him. Fleeing on foot after they were separated, Elm hijacked a car, only to be shot in the stomach by the terrified driver, whom Elm shot dead in return. 

Back in the warehouse, Cal returned. He listened coldly to Elm's account of Cedar's sudden death, walked over to Doyle, and shot the officer dead himself. 

Finally, Bram arrived. He pointed a finger at the dying undercover cop and named Elm as the informer. Ash refused to believe him, loyalty blinding him as he turned his gun directly on Bram. The resulting three-way standoff exploded into gunfire, leaving Bram, Cal, and Ash all shot on the concrete, with only Ash and Elm still breathing. 

Elm looked up at his protector and confessed the truth: he was a police officer. Ash stared in betrayal and shot Elm just as the tactical team stormed the warehouse, cutting Ash down in a hail of bullets.

Lena demanded that the man responsible be killed, so Aaron bought a gun and tracked Wes to a cheap highway motel. 

Wes Tarrow was an ex-convict, newly born again, who held down a steady job and coached boys' baseball, though his wife Nita secretly dreaded his sudden religious fanaticism and explosive temper. 

In a quiet suburb, Lena Ward lived a settled, gentle life alongside her husband Doug and their two young daughters, completely recovered from her former addictions. 

Far across the state, a mathematician named Aaron Vale sat in a sterile clinic, listening to a doctor explain that his failing heart would kill him within a matter of weeks unless a donor magically appeared. 

When grief finally tore her world apart, Lena surrendered to cocaine once more, methodically setting out to destroy herself. 

The turning point was a sudden collision at a pedestrian crossing: Wes’s pickup hit Doug and both little girls. Wes drove off in terror, turned back briefly to look, and then fled into the night. 

Before Aaron’s time ran out, his estranged wife Della pressed him relentlessly to consent to insemination using his frozen sperm so a piece of him might survive. 

In a quiet hospital waiting room, Lena was told the unbearable truth: her husband and both of her daughters were dead. 

Driven by an overwhelming wave of guilt, Wes walked straight into a police station, confessed to the hit-and-run, and was promptly sent back to prison. 

During a lengthy surgery, Doug’s heart was transplanted directly into Aaron’s chest, allowing the mathematician to wake up feeling truly alive for the first time in months. 

Haunted by the rhythmic thumping in his chest and unable to stop thinking about whose heart he had received, Aaron hired a private investigator to track down the donor’s widow. 

Upon his early release from prison, Wes abandoned his faith, walked out on Nita, and took a solitary job as a desk clerk at a distant roadside motel. 

Aaron eventually trailed Lena to a public swimming pool, engineered a seemingly casual meeting, and before long, the two began a passionate affair. 

Knowing his life was irrevocably altered, Aaron left Della, coldly telling her that he did not want the child she was desperately trying to conceive. 

Standing in the dim light outside the motel room, Aaron raised the gun but found himself completely unable to murder Wes; he merely wounded the ex-convict in the shoulder and urged him to run. 

Later, Aaron confessed the ultimate secret to Lena, admitting that he was carrying her late husband's heart inside him. She threw him out in a violent fury, only to succumb to her longing and take him back hours later. 

Bleeding and lost, Wes followed the pair back to their own motel room and begged Aaron to pull the trigger again to finish the job. Instead, overcome by horror, Aaron turned the gun on himself and pulled the trigger. 

Together, Lena and Wes loaded the dying mathematician into a car and rushed him to a nearby hospital, where the transplanted heart finally failed. His debt paid, Wes returned home to face his family, while a newly pregnant Lena walked back into the world alone.

Driven by an impulse he could not account for, Tobias skipped work and took the train to the coast, where he met a familiar-looking woman named Ivy on the frozen sand. They drove back to the city together in her car, and she invited him up to her flat.

Days before, Tobias had visited a bookshop only to find Ivy treating him like an absolute stranger while openly flirting with a young clerk named Peck. Devastated, he had learned that Ivy had hired a memory-erasure clinic to remove every trace of him from her mind. After Nina and Grady showed Tobias the form letter from the clinic, he marched straight to its director, Dr. Hallam, demanding the exact same procedure. Tobias boxed up every object connected with Ivy so the technicians could map the memories attached to them. That night, technicians Dell and Peck ran the overnight erasure in Tobias’s flat, though Peck quietly pocketed several mementos to use in wooing Ivy later. Inside his own mind, Tobias watched the most recent and ugliest memories dissolve around him one by one.

He remembered the final breakdown: Ivy coming home drunk after denting his car, sparking a blistering fight that ended with her walking out for good. Before that, their relationship had curdled into bitter recrimination over her drinking and his emotional withholding. 

In the flat, Dell and the receptionist Rosa got high on Tobias’s bed, losing track of the procedure while his neural map went off the rails. Reaching the deeper memories he still loved, Tobias changed his mind mid-process and tried to hide Ivy by smuggling her into old memories she was never part of. He clung to the two years they had fallen in love—skating on the ice of the frozen river, eating at the noodle house, and laughing at the drive-in. 

When Dr. Hallam arrived to re-map the crumbling erasure, Rosa impulsively kissed him, only for Hallam’s wife to reveal that Rosa’s own past affair with the doctor had already been erased. 

Farther back still, in the origin of it all, Tobias recalled meeting Ivy at a beach party at the end of the rail line, where they had broken into an empty house on the shore. In that last surviving memory inside the empty shore house, Tobias and Ivy said a final goodbye, and she whispered for him to meet her at the beach.

The erasure completed, and Tobias woke the next morning with no memory that Ivy had ever existed. 

Now, back in her flat after their unscripted reunion, a package arrived. Rosa had quit the clinic in disgust and mailed the files and audio tapes back to every patient on the books. Sitting together, Tobias and Ivy pressed play, listening in horror to their own recorded voices tearing each other apart. Ivy ran out into the hall, but after a moment, she returned. Looking at each other across the ruined slate of their minds, they agreed to try anyway.

Over breakfast in a quiet coffee shop, two small-time robbers chat over their coffee and decide on the spot to hold up the very diner they are sitting in.

Across the city, hitmen Rollo and Marcus drive through the streets, debating foreign drug laws and the peculiar names given to fast food abroad. Waiting in the dim corridor outside their target’s flat, they argue passionately over whether giving a foot massage is an act worth killing a man for. Once inside, Marcus recites a stern passage of scripture before the pair ruthlessly shoot a young man named Tobin for double-crossing their employer, Otis, and recover a locked briefcase. They deliver the briefcase to Otis at his bar, where the boss is paying the ageing boxer Denny to take a dive in the fifth round of his upcoming fight.

That night, Rollo buys heroin from his dealer Kip and shoots up before his night out. He takes Otis’s wife Nadia to a themed diner where they perform and win the venue's dance contest. Later, Nadia mistakenly snorts Rollo’s potent heroin, overdoses, and is narrowly revived by a frantic adrenaline shot delivered straight to her heart on the dealer's living-room floor.

Years earlier, a returning prisoner of war delivers to a young boy the gold watch his father kept hidden through long, agonizing years of captivity.

During the big fight, Denny double-crosses Otis, wins the match, and accidentally kills his opponent in the ring before escaping into the night in a taxi. Hiding in a secluded motel with his girlfriend Marielle, Denny discovers to his horror that she has left his father's watch behind in his flat. Denny returns to the apartment for the watch and shoots Rollo dead with a submachine gun left sitting on the kitchen counter. Escaping the scene, Denny and Otis collide in the street, crash their vehicles, and are taken prisoner in the basement of a pawnshop. Denny breaks free and comes back with a sword taken from the shop wall while one of their captors is raping Otis. Saved, Otis declares them square on the sole condition that Denny leaves town forever. Denny collects Marielle and rides out of the city on a motorcycle taken from the pawnshop.

Earlier that morning, back at the flat, a fourth man hidden in the bathroom had emptied a revolver at the hitmen without hitting either, an impossibility which Marcus immediately calls divine intervention. In the car afterwards, Rollo’s gun accidentally goes off and blows the head off their back-seat passenger, Del. Marcus parks the bloodied car at his friend Warren’s house, where an efficient fixer directs the cleanup and gives the two men fresh clothes.

Finally, back in the diner, Marcus talks the male robber down mid-holdup, hands over his own wallet while refusing to give up the briefcase, and lets the couple walk out unharmed.

Rex beat him down the concrete stairwell of the debt-record tower, throwing punches until the narrator tasted cold iron. To end the ghost commanding his hands, the narrator forced a handgun into his own mouth and pulled the trigger, the bullet tearing straight through his cheek and banishing Rex into the dark.

Long before the stairs, an insomniac product-recall investigator had discovered that the only thing allowing him to sleep was weeping in the arms of support groups for terminal diseases he did not have. Then Ada Vey began attending those exact same meetings. Her obvious, calculated faking shattered the fragile intimacy, destroying his only release.

Flight after flight filled his routine until he sat beside a soap salesman named Rex Marrow on a business trip and pocketed the man’s business card. Soon after, an unexplained explosion destroyed his high-rise flat along with every piece of catalogue furniture he owned. Desperate, he called Rex, who led him to a rotting, derelict house sitting at the edge of the industrial district. 

Outside a neighborhood bar, Rex turned to him and made a strange request: hit him as hard as he could. They beat each other bloody in the gravel car park, feeling alive for the first time. What started as two men brawling slowly hardened into a secret weekly basement club defined by its own strict rules, drawing in dozens of tired, angry men.

The house grew crowded when Ada overdosed, prompting Rex to carry her back to the derelict rooms, where the two began a loud, raw affair that the narrator could not stand to hear. Between their encounters, Rex rendered fat stolen from the dumpster of a cosmetic surgery clinic into pristine soap, selling it back to high-end department stores at eighty dollars a bar. Rex's control deepened the day he burned the narrator’s hand with raw lye, pinning him in place and refusing to let him retreat into peaceful meditation while his skin boiled. 

Using his own battered, swollen face as unspoken leverage, the narrator blackmailed his employer into paying him a full salary just to stay away from the office. Freed from work, Rex transformed the fight club into a disciplined underground organisation called Havoc, filling the derelict house with shaven-headed recruits who took silent orders and vandalised corporate property. The escalation reached a peak when Rex deliberately steered their car into oncoming traffic, let the vehicle roll into a ditch, and vanished into the night.

When a Havoc member named Ogden was shot dead by police during a midnight operation, horror set in, and the narrator started frantically trying to shut the entire network down. He travelled from city to city, only to find identical basement clubs everywhere he went, filled with strange men who greeted him respectfully as Rex Marrow. Piece by piece, the narrator worked out the terrifying truth: he and Rex were the exact same person, and Rex had been taking control of his body whenever he fell asleep. 

Ada confirmed it, admitting that she had been sleeping with him all along, not with a separate man named Rex. Driven by panic, the narrator discovered that Havoc had mined the central towers of the major debt-record companies, and he rushed into the basements to defuse the charges before it was too late.

After he shot himself through the cheek in the stairwell, Ada was brought into the high room, delivered to the tower by the shaven recruits. Standing together in the quiet room, their fingers intertwined, the two held hands at the massive window as the surrounding buildings imploded and fell into clouds of dust.

Ruben ran a red light at full speed, broadsiding Celine’s car in a deafening crunch of metal.

Before the collision, Ruben lived trapped in a cramped house alongside his mother, his brother Nestor, Nestor’s wife Alma, and their infant. Nestor spent his nights robbing pharmacies and his evenings beating Alma at home, prompting Ruben to repeatedly press her to run away with him. Searching for an escape, Ruben discovered that Nestor’s rottweiler, Tigre, killed other dogs on sight; he began entering the animal into local illegal dogfights, winning steadily. Desperate for freedom, Ruben paid two thugs to beat Nestor, but Nestor retaliated by taking Alma, the baby, and Ruben’s hidden savings before disappearing into the night. Months later, during a chaotic last fight, the promoter Chaco shot Tigre in the ring; Ruben stabbed Chaco in a fury and fled into the dark with his friend Pipo. Time passed until Nestor was shot dead while robbing a bank, and at the funeral, Ruben made one last offer to Alma to leave together, but she refused him completely.

In another part of the city, the model Celine Vaz had accepted a glamorous new life when her lover Hector walked out on his wife and daughters, moving Celine into a new flat facing a massive billboard of her own face. Following the brutal car crash, Celine woke in a hospital bed with her shattered leg pinned together, frantic to learn that her lapdog Chispa was lost somewhere back in the flat. As Chispa fell through a hole in the unbolted floorboards, Hector obsessively tore up the wooden floor to find the pet, oblivious as Celine’s pinned leg slowly turned gangrenous. Ultimately, Celine’s leg was amputated, and workers silently dismantled the billboard carrying her ruined image.

Across the city’s shadow world, a businessman named Elian hired Cardo to murder his half-brother and business partner, Sergio. Cardo, however, was preoccupied with ghost of his past; he watched silently from a distance as his estranged wife was buried in a bleak graveyard, afterward following his grown daughter Perla back to her home without revealing himself. 

His path had crossed the crash site weeks earlier. Cardo, a former guerrilla turned vagrant contract killer, happened to be standing at the junction during the wreck and pulled the bleeding rottweiler Tigre from the twisted steel. In his secluded yard, Cardo carefully nursed Tigre back to health among his own pack of strays. Yet the dog’s violent nature remained absolute; while Cardo was out one afternoon, Tigre slaughtered every other dog in the yard. Returning to the bloodbath, Cardo put a gun directly to the rottweiler's head, but found he could not pull the trigger.

Instead of carrying out his assignment, Cardo abducted Sergio, but chained him up alive inside his hidden lair instead of killing him. Soon after, Cardo brought Elian face to face with his captive brother, dropped a loaded pistol on the floor between them, and walked out into the night having pocketed money from both men. Seeking a final absolution, Cardo broke into Perla’s flat while she was away, left a long confession detailing his true identity on her answering machine, and stole a small photograph of her from the table. Shaved smooth and dressed in clean clothes, Cardo left all his blood money behind for Perla and walked out into the vast wasteland, accompanied only by Tigre.

In a quiet flat high above the neon-drenched pavement, an old man stood at the window, gesturing down toward the dark city as he explained to a younger man that nothing ever truly survives time. 

Down in the street below them, red and blue lights flickered against the bricks as police officers handcuffed Cort and Jonah, dragging the two young men out through the heavy doors of the night club. 

Inside the music-throbbing venue, minutes earlier, Jonah had grabbed a heavy red fire extinguisher and smashed a man's face into a bloody pulp. He had no idea that the real rapist, a local pimp known as the Adder, stood mere feet away in the shadows, silently watching the brutal mistake unfold. 

Cort had been the one to start it all, hunting frantically through the dark crowds of the club until he seized a man he believed was the assailant, only for the stranger to twist his grip and snap Cort’s arm with a sudden, sickening crack. 

Before entering the gloom of the Pit, two men on the street had approached Cort, offering to sell him the rapist’s name for a price and steering him and Jonah directly toward the subterranean venue. 

Hours before that desperate search, Cort and Jonah had emerged from the noise of a house party into the cool night air, only to freeze as they watched paramedics load a battered, unconscious Lise into the back of an ambulance. 

She had been lying broken in the concrete gloom of an isolated tunnel. There, the Adder had raped her, violently bouncing her head against the hard floor while a lone passer-by happened upon the scene, gasped in horror, and hurriedly backed away into the shadows. 

Lise had only gone down there because she had wanted to avoid crossing a roaring, busy thoroughfare, taking the pedestrian underpass instead. Walking into the tiled corridor, she had stumbled directly upon the Adder in the middle of viciously beating a transsexual woman. 

Earlier that evening, Lise had been at the party, watching in growing disgust as Cort got steadily drunk and high, openly flirting with and pursuing other women. Unable to stand the sight of him any longer, she turned on her heel and left the house entirely on her own. 

They had all arrived together on the underground, squashed into the fluorescent carriage with Jonah, cheerfully arguing and laughing about sex and teasing Cort about his heavy drinking. 

Before that night out, Lise had been lying tangled in the bedsheets beside Cort, describing a vivid, recurring dream she kept having about a long red tunnel, while the two of them playfully teased each other about her lingering history with Jonah. 

Long before that bedroom conversation, Lise had stood alone in her quiet flat, waiting in the stillness until the plastic stick in her hand revealed two distinct lines, confirming her positive pregnancy test. 

And earlier still, on a bright and peaceful afternoon, Lise sat on a wooden bench in the park. Cool water from the sprinklers misted the air as children laughed and played across the lawn, while she turned the pages of her book, one hand resting softly on her stomach.

Martin drew his weapon and shot Roy through the head in the derelict building, taking a quick instant photograph of the corpse before the memory could vanish from his mind.

In a quiet motel room he could not remember checking into, Martin sat on the bed with the phone pressed to his ear, slowly narrating the file of Elias Prine to an anonymous caller.

Earlier that day, Corinne ran a licence plate number through a friend working at the vehicle registry, eventually handing Martin an official record naming Roy Mercer.

Years earlier, working as an insurance investigator, Martin Kray had personally interviewed a claimant named Elias Prine, ruling the man's severe memory loss psychosomatic and officially denying the claim.

Tracking a new lead, Martin ambushed Vance inside a motel bathroom, mercilessly beating the man before driving him out of town at gunpoint.

Decades prior, Elias's diabetic wife had decided to test him by repeatedly asking for injection after injection, ultimately dying of the severe insulin overdose he could not remember giving her.

Scheming against him, Corinne hid every single pen in her house to cut off his notes, goaded Martin into hitting her, and then returned looking bruised to blame a man called Vance so that Martin would aggressively pursue him.

To navigate his broken mind, Martin painstakingly built a rigid system of instant photographs, annotated notes, and permanent body tattoos to hunt down the second attacker, a mysterious figure known only by the initials R.M.

At her bar, Gil's girlfriend Corinne instantly recognised the dead man's tailored clothes and custom sports car, bitterly serving Martin a glass of beer that her staff had secretly spat in.

His existence had fractured the night intruders viciously attacked Martin and his wife inside their own bathroom; Martin managed to kill one of the men, but a violent strike to his head stole his ability to ever form new memories again.

Driven by his rigid system, Martin drove to a local tattoo parlour and had the plate number inked directly onto his thigh as his unshakeable sixth fact.

Out in an isolated field, Martin burned his late wife's personal hairbrush and books, desperately attempting to grieve a tragic loss that he could never retain.

Over the line, the caller fed Martin a specific name and location, formally identifying the drug dealer Gil Marsh as the exact man he was looking for.

Martin cornered and ambushed Gil in a dark, derelict basement, beating and strangling him to death before taking a photo of the lifeless body.

As he died, Gil weakly whispered the word "Elias"—a detail Martin could not possibly explain—before Martin stripped the body, changed into the dead man's suit, and took off in his sports car.

Roy suddenly arrived on the scene and broke the news, telling Martin that Gil was entirely innocent, that Martin had already avenged his wife a year ago, and that Martin himself was actually the man in the Prine story.

About a year before the main action, a plainclothes officer called Roy had helped Martin track down and kill the real attacker, an act of bloody vengeance that Martin completely forgot within minutes.

Rather than believe a word of it, Martin burned his photographs of Gil, wrote "he is lying to you" across Roy's picture, and carefully copied down Roy's licence plate as his next target.

Detective Isaiah Reece stepped past the police tape into the freezing damp of the roadside brush. A body lay slumped against the embankment, cold and silent. When Reece pulled back the yellow blanket, his heart seized; the dead young man staring blankly at the sky was his own brother, Kwame.

Months before that terrible dawn, an immigrant shopkeeper named Nadir stood in a dimly lit gun shop with his daughter Sahar, purchasing a cheap handgun while the dealer openly mocked his accent.

That same evening outside a crowded restaurant, Trey and Kwame ambushed prosecutor Halstead and carjacked his luxury sedan. 

The following morning, locksmith Mateo replaced the locks on the Halstead home. As he worked, Paula Halstead loudly complained to her husband that the workman was surely a gang member who would sell duplicate keys to criminals.

Later that afternoon, Officer Boyle pulled over Clay and Renee Hobart. Boyle forced Renee from the vehicle and groped her degraded body in front of her furious husband before letting them go with a harsh warning. 

Sickened by the encounter, Boyle's partner Voss went straight to their commander, demanding a new patrol car rather than spending another shift riding with an unrepentant racist.

Mateo went on to replace the lock on Nadir’s corner store, explicitly warning him that the wooden door frame was broken and insecure. Nadir flew into a rage, accusing the locksmith of running a con to overcharge him.

Desperate to save his dying father, Boyle pleaded with health insurance clerk Delia Frank for essential treatment, but she coldly refused his request.

That night, Nadir's shop was smashed open and thoroughly looted; the insurance company refused to pay a dime because he had ignored Mateo's warning about the broken door.

Cruising the city in another stolen vehicle, Trey and Kwame struck a shopkeeper named Pham and hastily dumped his broken body outside a hospital entrance.

Meanwhile, Renee Hobart found herself pinned upside down inside a burning vehicle wreck, screaming in terror until Officer Boyle—the very man who had assaulted her—crawled into the flames and dragged her to safety.

When Clay Hobart was stopped by police mid-carjacking while attempting to recover his stolen vehicle, Officer Voss intervened, talking the tense officers out of shooting him.

Terrified and panicked, Clay drove away at high speed with Trey in the passenger seat, evading the police before violently throwing Trey out onto the pavement.

Racked with ruin and vengeance, Nadir waited in the shadows outside Mateo's home with his handgun. The moment Mateo stepped onto the porch, Nadir pulled the trigger just as Mateo's small daughter Rosie ran out into her father's arms.

The little girl was untouched; Sahar had secretly purchased blanks, and Nadir collapsed in tears, believing the child was his angel.

Out on a dark rural road, Voss picked up Kwame hitchhiking. When Kwame reached into his jacket pocket, Voss misread the movement, shot him dead, and set the car on fire to hide the crime.

At Kwame's memorial, Reece's mother wept uncontrollably, blaming Isaiah for never once going out to look for his lost brother.

Days later, Paula Halstead fell down her grand staircase. Bruised and helpless on the floor, she looked up at her housekeeper Alba and wept that she was the only friend she had left in the world.

Searching for a payout, Trey discovered Pham's parked van crammed with trafficked migrants, but instead of selling them to another ring, he drove them to the docks and released them all.

As the first snow of the year began to fall over the city, another violent collision echoed through the intersection, starting another furious argument in the street.

The draft came through without notice, a sudden transfer that shipped a new chaplain's assistant overseas with no training worth the name.

On a distant world, he was kept in a zoo behind transparent walls alongside a film actress, under the gaze of alien onlookers.

Before any of that, a boy was born in a small industrial town, growing into a weak, peculiar child who spent his early years largely unnoticed.

Later, he was sent on to a great city and housed alongside other prisoners in a disused abattoir that smelled faintly of old blood.

When he finally came home from the war, he collapsed instantly and was hospitalised, where a patient in the adjacent bed introduced him to a hack science fiction writer.

It was during his captivity that the aliens had explained their view of reality to him, demonstrating how every moment exists at once and how free will is an idea peculiar to his own planet.

He remembered being lost behind the lines with a scout who beat him mercilessly for wanting to be left to die in the snow.

Years meant little when he married the daughter of the man who owned the optometry school, an alliance that quickly made him rich.

In the middle of his life, the great city was destroyed by fire in one night, and the prisoners sheltering in the deep meat locker came up to find the entire world gone.

Decades faded together until his daughter decided he was senile and took his affairs out of his hands, filing papers to manage his life.

The memory of the water was equally vivid, of the day his father threw him into the deep end of a pool to teach him to swim, though he merely sank straight to the bottom.

On the prison train, he watched the scout die of gangrene in the corner of a crowded boxcar, blaming him with his last rasping breath.

He found himself sitting on a radio talk show, trying to tell the skeptical host and the world about the aliens and the structure of the fourth dimension.

He was back in the ruins after the fire, where the surviving prisoners were made to dig bodies out of the cellars until one of the diggers died of the dry heaves.

He survived an air crash in the cold mountains, never knowing until much later that his wife had died of carbon monoxide poisoning from exhaust fumes while driving to the hospital.

He spent months held in a camp beside enemy officers who had been drawing double rations for years through a clerical error that no one ever caught.

Eventually, he was shot dead by a beam weapon after addressing a crowd, falling to the pavement exactly as he had always known he would be.

A fellow prisoner had promised to have him killed one day on the dead scout's account, a promise that floated without time alongside every other moment he had ever inhabited.

In the dim light of a quiet bar, two years after everything had drifted to a halt, Odile sat across from Wilder. She told him flatly that her marriage to Emlyn was over, adding that she had spent the previous night confessing every detail of their old affair to her husband. As they talked, Odile let slip a piece of news: Emlyn had recently been publishing a certain novelist—a writer Wilder represented, though both men had quietly detested the author for years.

The revelation threw Wilder into a panicked state. That very evening, he rang Emlyn in distress, begging him to come over. Emlyn arrived at Wilder’s house without hesitation. Sitting across from his old friend, Emlyn admitted calmly that he had known about the affair for four years already, ever since his wife had told him during a trip abroad. He added dryly that he had never thought much of Wilder's letters, either.

Before that night, time had simply unspooled backward through its quiet indignities. Prior to their final unraveling, Wilder and Odile had agreed that keeping their secret apartment had become a tedious chore; together, they split up the crockery they had bought and surrendered the lease. Months before the lease was given up, the two men had sat over dinner at the married couple's house, endlessly debating racquet games and schoolboy athletics until Odile was completely excluded from the conversation. 

Earlier still, in a hotel lobby during a trip abroad, Emlyn had paused at the front desk to ask Odile about a letter held for her, written in a hand he recognized immediately. Trapped, Odile confessed the truth then and there. Emlyn offered no rage, only remarking coolly that he had always been far fonder of his friend than of his wife.

Upon returning from that foreign journey, Odile went straight back to the rented rooms. She said nothing whatever about the trip or her confession, and the afternoon passed exactly as every other afternoon had passed before it. Not long after, Emlyn sat through a long, boozy restaurant lunch with Wilder, drinking heavily while baiting the agent about the failures of contemporary fiction, never once mentioning a single word of what he had learned abroad.

Years before the truth was aired, Wilder and Odile had first taken those very rooms in a quiet district. They had eagerly filled the space with fine linen and stacks of plates, intentionally giving their secret affair a tangible household of its own. It was in those freshly furnished rooms that Odile eventually announced she was carrying her husband's child. After a quiet deliberation, the pair had decided that the rented rooms would go on exactly as before, untouched by the coming child.

And long before any apartment was rented, before the linen was folded or the letters written, there had been a party at the house of Emlyn, Wilder’s closest friend. While the other guests laughed and drank on the floor downstairs, Wilder, a young book agent, had taken Odile by the hand, led her into a quiet upstairs room, and softly told her how lovely she was.

She told him flatly that her marriage to Emlyn was over, adding that she had spent the previous night confessing every detail of their old affair to her husband. As they talked, Odile let slip a piece of news: Emlyn had recently been publishing a certain novelist—a writer Wilder represented, though both men had quietly detested the author for years.

The revelation threw Wilder into a panicked state. That very evening, he rang Emlyn in distress, begging him to come over. Emlyn arrived at Wilder’s house without hesitation. Sitting across from his old friend, Emlyn admitted calmly that he had known about the affair for four years already, ever since his wife had told him during a trip abroad. He added dryly that he had never thought much of Wilder's letters, either.

Before that night, time had simply unspooled backward through its quiet indignities. Prior to their final unraveling, Wilder and Odile had agreed that keeping their secret apartment had become a tedious chore; together, they split up the crockery they had bought and surrendered the lease. Months before the lease was given up, the two men had sat over dinner at the married couple's house, endlessly debating racquet games and schoolboy athletics until Odile was completely excluded from the conversation. 

Earlier still, in a hotel lobby during a trip abroad, Emlyn had paused at the front desk to ask Odile about a letter held for her, written in a hand he recognized immediately. Trapped, Odile confessed the truth then and there. Emlyn offered no rage, only remarking coolly that he had always been far fonder of his friend than of his wife.

Upon returning from that foreign journey, Odile went straight back to the rented rooms. She said nothing whatever about the trip or her confession, and the afternoon passed exactly as every other afternoon had passed before it. Not long after, Emlyn sat through a long, boozy restaurant lunch with Wilder, drinking heavily while baiting the agent about the failures of contemporary fiction, never once mentioning a single word of what he had learned abroad.

Years before the truth was aired, Wilder and Odile had first taken those very rooms in a quiet district. They had eagerly filled the space with fine linen and stacks of plates, intentionally giving their secret affair a tangible household of its own. It was in those freshly furnished rooms that Odile eventually announced she was carrying her husband's child. After a quiet deliberation, the pair had decided that the rented rooms would go on exactly as before, untouched by the coming child.

And long before any apartment was rented, before the linen was folded or the letters written, there had been a party at the house of Emlyn, Wilder’s closest friend. While the other guests laughed and drank on the floor downstairs, Wilder, a young book agent, had taken Odile by the hand, led her into a quiet upstairs room, and softly told her how lovely she was.

Helicopters droned through the night, spraying the entire city to eradicate crop pests as they passed over every neighborhood. Beneath that low hum, Doctor Neil Hartigan and his wife Bess, a painter, got ready for an upcoming dinner party. In another room across town, Cheryl, a telephone-sex worker, talked men through their explicit fantasies from her living room armchair while her husband Stu sat beside her, seething in silent fury. Farther downtown, the singer Vida performed nightly in a dimly lit club, unaware that her cellist daughter Bee was at home playing her instrument in absolute solitude. Meanwhile, Officer Rowe, secretly cheating on his wife Peg with a woman named Nan, deliberately abandoned his family's dog in a distant neighborhood just to cover up one of his tangled lies.

The next morning, young Charlie Rill was knocked down by a car driven by a waitress named Rhona on his way to school, though he picked himself up and walked home insisting he was entirely fine. Around that time, the baker Otto Kemp took an order over the counter for a birthday cake meant for Charlie. Soon after arriving home, Charlie collapsed into a deep coma, leaving his desperate parents, Grant and Elaine, to keep a silent vigil beside his hospital bed. Across the district, Ike and Dot house-sat in the empty Hartigan residence, entertaining themselves by taking photographs of Dot meticulously made up to resemble a beaten corpse.

Out in the wilderness, Stu and three of his friends drove up to a remote river to fish, only to discover a young woman’s body floating face down near the bank. Back in the city, Nan's ex-husband Cass, a spray helicopter pilot, learned that she was seeing a new man, and in a violent rage, he sawed her living room furniture into jagged pieces. At the same time, receiving neither payment nor an explanation for the unclaimed birthday cake, Otto the baker grew bitter and began making anonymous, menacing phone calls to the grieving Rill house. Out at the river, Stu and his companions tied the floating body securely to the bank with rope and casually carried on fishing for two more days before finally notifying anyone. 

Inside the hospital room, Grant's estranged father Duff unexpectedly turned up, sitting by his comatose grandson while confessing a secret affair he had conducted decades ago. When news of the fishing trip eventually broke, Vern's wife Iris, who worked as a children's party clown, was deeply disgusted to learn what her husband and the other men had done. Later that evening at the Hartigans' dinner party, Bess publicly admitted to a long-ago nude modelling session and a past affair, driving Neil to fly into a rage and make an embarrassing scene. 

In the quiet hours that followed, little Charlie died in his hospital bed. Consumed by anger and grief, Grant and Elaine drove straight to the bakery to confront Otto, but the baker simply fed them warm, freshly baked bread and grieved beside them in shared sorrow. Late that night, Bee found her mother Vida fast asleep, walked silently out to the garage, closed the heavy door behind her, and killed herself with the car engine running. The following afternoon, during a bright picnic up in the hills, Stu suddenly snapped and smashed a young woman's head with a heavy rock. Moments later, a powerful tremor shook the entire city, and every recent death, violent act, and tragic wreck was folded into a single, overwhelming evening news bulletin.

Dressed in solemn robes as devout pilgrims, Solly Two Coats and his crew robbed a high-security diamond house in a northern port, walking casually out into the damp mist carrying a massive, priceless stone. Miles away, the sleek boxing promoters Halloway and Digby sent their prized fighter, Pretty Sam, down to a muddy camp of travellers to purchase a caravan. The negotiation turned sour in seconds when a local bare-knuckle fighter named Finn knocked Sam out cold over the deal, leaving Halloway suddenly without a man to fight in gang boss Coldstone’s heavily fixed bout. Overseas, Solly’s cousin Marv caught wind of the score and told Solly to bring the stone straight over without delay. Backed into a corner, Halloway had no choice but to put Finn into the fight instead, promising the terrifying Coldstone that Finn would go down on cue in the fourth round.

Hoping to make a bit extra on the side, Grigor the Nail told Solly about a high-stakes bookmaker's in the city, but at the exact same time, he tipped off the pawnbrokers Ike and Benno to rob Solly right outside the shop. Solly landed in the city, delivered the diamond safely to the fence Hersch, and headed straight for the bookmaker's to bet on the fight. Inside the ring, however, Finn paid no mind to the arrangement and knocked his opponent out cold in the very first round. Coldstone lost a massive fortune on the upset and viciously took his rage out on Halloway. Immediately following the match, Ike, Benno, and Tulley bungled their opportunistic robbery outside, managing only to slice off Solly's arm to free his locked briefcase before an armed Grigor chased them off.

Marv flew into the country shortly after, only to find Solly gone, prompting him to hire the relentless bounty hunter Ledge to find his cousin. Grigor intercepted the crippled Solly first, cutting off his remaining arm to force the briefcase open, only to suffer the bitter realization that the stone was not inside it. Coldstone soon intervened, feeding the tragic Solly to his prized pigs before sternly showing Halloway and Digby what would happen to them if the second fight went wrong. Meanwhile, Ledge successfully traced the pawnbrokers, shooting their getaway car to pieces and taking both the thieves and the stone into his custody.

Desperate to survive, Halloway and Digby ordered Finn to go down in the fourth round as instructed, while Coldstone’s heavy-handed men made sure of his compliance by setting fire to a caravan and burning Finn's mother to death. The brutal conflict spilled onto the highway when Grigor ambushed Ledge's car while Ike and Benno were trapped inside; during the chaotic shootout that followed, Ledge, Grigor, and Benno were all killed. Amidst the gunfire and corpses, Tulley quietly slipped away into the night with a stray dog that had swallowed the loose diamond during the fray.

The night of the second fight arrived, but a grief-stricken Finn refused to bend, knocking his opponent out cold once again in the fourth round, which triggered a riot as the travellers in the crowd mercilessly massacred Coldstone's men. Capitalizing on the violence, Halloway and Digby cornered Coldstone and shot him dead, and by the time morning broke over the blood-soaked arena, the travellers had vanished without a trace. A short while later, the stray dog was handed in at a neighbourhood pet shop, where it suddenly coughed up the stolen diamond, leaving Halloway and Digby holding the fortune they had suffered so much to find.
